name: What taking a job costs you
description:
This indicator measures the financial disincentives to participate in the labour market. It calculates the proportion of earnings in the new job that are lost to either higher taxes or lower benefit entitlements when a jobless person takes up employment and claims unemployment benefits. Higher values means higher financial disincentives.

Calculations for families with children assume 2 children aged 4 and 6 who do not use formal childcare.

desc_html:
What happens to your income when you take a job. The number is the share of the earnings from a new job that never reaches you, because taxes start and benefits stop at the same time. At 100 per cent, working leaves you no better off than not working.
This is the measurable core of the argument about whether benefits discourage work, and the answer is not the one either side usually assumes: rates are high almost everywhere, and they are highest for the people entering low-paid work, not for high earners.
The Contribution dial breaks the rate into its causes -- taxes starting, benefits withdrawn, childcare fees beginning. For a lone parent taking a minimum-wage job, childcare fees alone often exceed everything the tax system takes.
Switch Benefit type between unemployment insurance and guaranteed minimum income, and set how long the person has been out of work. Under Advanced are the assumptions behind the simulation: whether housing benefit and social assistance top-ups are claimed, whether childcare is used, and the ages of the children.
These are modelled households, not survey observations. OECD computes what its tax-benefit rules imply for a specified family in a specified situation.
desc_text: The share of earnings from a new job lost to taxes starting and benefits stopping, for modelled households leaving unemployment or minimum income.
source_notes: These are simulations from OECD's tax-benefit models, not observations of real households. They assume full take-up of every benefit the household is entitled to, which real take-up never reaches, so they overstate what an average claimant actually loses by starting work.

Regional rows such as OECD, EU27 and G7 are compiled from whichever member countries reported that particular figure in that particular year, so what they cover changes between one selection and the next. Two things follow. A breakdown can exceed the total it belongs to, because the two are built from different sets of countries. And a count for a region can come out far too small, because only some members reported it. Compare countries directly where the question allows it; read the regional rows as a rough centre of gravity rather than as a measurement of the region.
